power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: This chapter describes a neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) approach to cognitive rehabilitation (CR) following acquired brain injury (ABI), with primary emphasis on traumatic brain injury and stroke.

NIPE is conceptualised as more than information provision: neuroscience-informed explanations are used to help patients and families understand cognitive difficulties, recovery, rehabilitation strategies, and their implications for everyday functioning.
Neuropsychological feedback is presented as a common context for NIPE, with attention to tailoring, functional translation, multimodal support, and verification of understanding.
A dual-lens framework is proposed for NIPE delivery in CR.
The therapeutic lens emphasises alliance, empathy and warmth, person-centred collaboration, shared explanatory models, and goal setting.

The cognition-informed lens addresses how cognitive difficulties may affect learning through adjustment of information load and pacing, repetition, clear and concrete language, integration with existing knowledge, teach-back, and multimodal delivery.

Together, these lenses inform considerations of timing and context and seven structural principles of NIPE: trustworthiness, interaction, salience, motivation, intensity, repetition, and multimodal/multimedia delivery.
The chapter also considers NIPE content related to neuroplasticity, prognosis and recovery, rehabilitation approaches, and factors that may influence functioning and participation.
Throughout, emphasis is placed on distinguishing established evidence from plausible but untested mechanisms and on presenting recovery in probabilistic rather than deterministic terms.

Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) can be used within cognitive rehabilitation following acquired brain injury (ABI) to help patients and families develop a workable understanding of what has changed, why difficulties may be occurring, and what can be done to support functioning in everyday life.

Following ABI, cognitive difficulties such as slowed processing, attentional impairment, and reduced new learning can affect how information is acquired and retained (Maas et al., 2022; El Husseini et al., 2023).

text.text: The manner in which information is presented is therefore clinically important.
In this context, NIPE may support self-awareness, realistic expectations about recovery, understanding of rehabilitation strategies, and engagement in treatment.

This chapter considers NIPE within cognitive rehabilitation, with particular emphasis on traumatic brain injury (TBI) and stroke, and describes neuropsychological feedback as a common context for its delivery.
Building on the foundational NIPE framework introduced in Chapter 1 (Rezapour et al., 2026), this chapter applies NIPE specifically to cognitive rehabilitation following ABI.

text.text: A dual-lens framework is proposed for this purpose.
The therapeutic lens emphasises alliance, empathy and warmth, person-centred collaboration, shared explanatory models, and goal setting.
The cognition-informed lens considers how cognitive difficulties affect the acquisition, retention, and application of new information.

Together, these lenses inform considerations of timing and context and seven structural principles of NIPE: trustworthiness, interaction, salience, motivation, intensity, repetition, and multimodal/ multimedia delivery.
These principles provide a practical framework for delivering information in ways that are credible, understandable, memorable, and relevant to everyday functioning.
This chapter focuses primarily on TBI and stroke because both are common forms of ABI and have substantial cognitive rehabilitation literatures.
Other causes of ABI include hypoxic-ischaemic or anoxic injury, central nervous system infection, brain tumours and their treatment, and toxic or metabolic insults.

Although cognitive rehabilitation has also been applied to other neurological conditions, including dementia (Kudlicka et al., 2023), and broader cognition-oriented interventions have been studied across other older adult populations (Gavelin et al., 2020), these populations are beyond the scope of this chapter.

text.text: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) refers to an acquired disruption of brain function caused by an external mechanical force.

Its cognitive, emotional, behavioural, and physical consequences vary according to factors such as injury severity and characteristics, premorbid functioning, and the broader clinical and psychosocial context (Maas et al., 2022; Rauchman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Its cognitive, emotional, behavioural, and physical consequences vary according to factors such as injury severity and characteristics, premorbid functioning, and the broader clinical and psychosocial context <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Maas et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Rauchman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive sequelae may include difficulties with attention, processing speed, memory and new learning, executive functioning, and social cognition.

Emotional and behavioural changes are also common and can include depression, anxiety, irritability, emotional lability, fatigue, sleep disturbance, post-traumatic stress symptoms, impulsivity, disinhibition, apathy, and reduced frustration tolerance.
Moderate to severe TBI may also affect self-awareness and self-monitoring.
Longer-term consequences can include changes in social participation, relationships, and behaviour (Maas et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Longer-term consequences can include changes in social participation, relationships, and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Maas et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Stroke results from cerebral infarction or haemorrhage and can produce focal neurological and cognitive impairments depending on the location and extent of injury (Sacco et al., 2013; Coupland et al., 2017; Hilkens et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Stroke results from cerebral infarction or haemorrhage and can produce focal neurological and cognitive impairments depending on the location and extent of injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Sacco et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Coupland et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hilkens et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Major stroke subtypes include ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Ischaemic strokes account for most strokes and result from interruption of blood flow, whereas haemorrhagic strokes result from bleeding within or around the brain.
Post-stroke cognitive impairment is common and can affect processing speed, attention, memory, executive functioning, language, and visuospatial abilities (El Husseini et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Post-stroke cognitive impairment is common and can affect processing speed, attention, memory, executive functioning, language, and visuospatial abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(El Husseini et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The pattern of impairment varies with lesion location and distributed network involvement.
Emotional sequelae, including depression and anxiety, are also common (Chun et al., 2022).

text.text: Impaired awareness or anosognosia may occur in some patients and can affect safety, goal setting, and participation in rehabilitation (Orfei et al., 2007).

text.text: NIPE content focuses on brain-based explanations of the mechanisms and symptoms of brain disorders, as well as the neural processes associated with treatment response, remission, and recovery (Rezapour et al., 2026).
text.formatted: NIPE content focuses on brain-based explanations of the mechanisms and symptoms of brain disorders, as well as the neural processes associated with treatment response, remission, and recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rezapour et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this chapter, the emphasis is specifically on neuroscience-informed explanations relevant to recovery and rehabilitation following acquired brain injury.
The mechanisms and symptoms of acquired brain injury are addressed elsewhere in this volume.
Psychoeducation provided as part of cognitive rehabilitation is often neuroscience-informed, but the inclusion of brain-related information alone does not necessarily make an intervention NIPE.

Within cognitive rehabilitation, NIPE refers more specifically to the deliberate use of neuroscience-informed explanations to help patients understand how brain function relates to cognitive difficulties, rehabilitation strategies, and everyday functioning (Rezapour et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Within cognitive rehabilitation, NIPE refers more specifically to the deliberate use of neuroscience-informed explanations to help patients understand how brain function relates to cognitive difficulties, rehabilitation strategies, and everyday functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rezapour et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, NIPE extends beyond information provision by helping patients develop a more coherent and personally meaningful understanding of both their difficulties and the rehabilitation process.
Accordingly, neither neuropsychological feedback nor cognitive rehabilitation should be considered NIPE simply because neuroscience is discussed.

What distinguishes NIPE is the purposeful use of neuroscience-informed explanations to support understanding and rehabilitation, together with attention to how that information is structured and delivered.
Cognitive rehabilitation provides a natural context for NIPE because it explicitly links brain function to everyday behavior.

By making these relationships understandable and personally relevant, NIPE may support mechanistic self-awareness by helping patients recognize patterns of cognitive difficulty and anticipate their impact.

It may also strengthen the rationale for rehabilitation strategies by linking specific techniques to underlying cognitive processes and clarifying when and why those strategies may be useful across contexts.

In addition, NIPE may help align expectations about recovery and support motivation and persistence by framing recovery as a process that can involve neural adaptation, learning, compensation, and adjustment rather than as a fixed limitation.
Together, these proposed pathways suggest that NIPE may function as an active component of rehabilitation rather than solely as a supplementary source of information.
Psychoeducation can occur throughout cognitive rehabilitation, but neuropsychological assessment feedback provides a natural entry point for NIPE.
Early work emphasised the clinical importance of communicating neuropsychological findings in ways that patients and families could understand and use (Gass and Brown, 1992).
text.formatted: Early work emphasised the clinical importance of communicating neuropsychological findings in ways that patients and families could understand and use <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gass and Brown, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Consumer research also identified variability in whether feedback was provided and whether patients experienced it as useful and understandable, highlighting the importance of clear and meaningful communication of assessment findings (Bennett-Levy et al., 1994).
text.formatted: Consumer research also identified variability in whether feedback was provided and whether patients experienced it as useful and understandable, highlighting the importance of clear and meaningful communication of assessment findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bennett-Levy et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Subsequent collaborative and therapeutic assessment models increasingly conceptualised assessment feedback as a potentially therapeutic process rather than solely as the communication of test results (Fischer, 2000; Gorske, 2008).

text.text: Early empirical work on assessment feedback consisted largely of consumer and practitioner surveys addressing satisfaction, perceived usefulness, and clinical practice (Bennett-Levy et al., 1994; Smith et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Early empirical work on assessment feedback consisted largely of consumer and practitioner surveys addressing satisfaction, perceived usefulness, and clinical practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bennett-Levy et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Smith et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: More recent studies have examined broader outcomes.

In an observational study, patients who attended neuropsychological feedback reported greater improvement in quality of life, understanding of their condition, and ability to cope than patients who did not receive direct feedback (Rosado et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In an observational study, patients who attended neuropsychological feedback reported greater improvement in quality of life, understanding of their condition, and ability to cope than patients who did not receive direct feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rosado et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from controlled research is more limited.

A randomised controlled crossover trial in multiple sclerosis found no between-group improvement at one week in knowledge of cognitive functioning or coping, although within-subject analyses at one month showed improvements in perceived cognitive functioning, self-efficacy, stress, and depression (Longley et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A randomised controlled crossover trial in multiple sclerosis found no between-group improvement at one week in knowledge of cognitive functioning or coping, although within-subject analyses at one month showed improvements in perceived cognitive functioning, self-efficacy, stress, and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Longley et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest potential benefits of feedback while also highlighting the limited and heterogeneous evidence regarding specific therapeutic effects.

A major scoping review found considerable heterogeneity in neuropsychological feedback methods and outcomes but identified several convergent practice recommendations, including tailoring information to the individual, translating findings into everyday functioning, involving family or support persons when appropriate, using multimodal materials, and checking understanding (Gruters et al., 2022).

text.text: A more recent clinical review similarly emphasises neuropsychological feedback as a therapeutic communication process in which the way information is conveyed can influence understanding and followthrough (Armstrong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A more recent clinical review similarly emphasises neuropsychological feedback as a therapeutic communication process in which the way information is conveyed can influence understanding and followthrough <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Armstrong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Neuropsychological feedback is now common in neuropsychological practice, although its format, duration, and supporting materials vary across settings and patient populations (Smith et al., 2007; McRae et al., 2024).

text.text: Efforts to improve consistency have included development of the PsyCET-F, a competency framework for feedback delivery intended for use in training, clinical practice, and research (Wong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Efforts to improve consistency have included development of the PsyCET-F, a competency framework for feedback delivery intended for use in training, clinical practice, and research <ref type="bibr">(Wong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In a recent expert consensus study, the highest-rated potential outcomes of neuropsychological assessment were improved patient or caregiver understanding of presenting problems, improved understanding of how to manage and cope with cognitive symptoms, and diagnostic clarification (Wong et al., 2026).

text.text: From a NIPE perspective, neuropsychological feedback provides a useful opportunity to connect assessment findings with cognitive processes and everyday functioning.

These explanations may help patients develop a more coherent and actionable understanding of their cognitive strengths and difficulties, which can in turn inform goal setting, strategy selection, and participation in rehabilitation.
The delivery of NIPE in cognitive rehabilitation can be considered through two complementary and overlapping lenses.
A therapeutic lens emphasizes the interpersonal and motivational conditions that support engagement, including alliance, collaboration, shared explanatory models, and goal setting.
A cognition-informed lens considers how cognitive difficulties following ABI affect the acquisition, retention, and application of new information.

Together, these lenses inform considerations of timing and context and seven principles of NIPE delivery: trustworthiness, interaction, salience, motivation, intensity, repetition, and multimodal/ multimedia delivery.
Table 1 provides a proposed clinician-facing framework summarizing how the overlapping perspectives of the two lenses contribute to each principle and their implications for clinical delivery.

text.text: NIPE content should be tailored to the stage of recovery following ABI, while recognizing that recovery trajectories and information needs vary considerably across individuals.

text.text: Psychoeducation may therefore be most useful when its amount, depth, and focus are matched to the person's current needs and readiness rather than delivered according to a fixed schedule.
Introducing difficult or complex information gradually may also help patients and families integrate new understanding as recovery and adjustment unfold (Postal and Armstrong, 2013).
text.formatted: Introducing difficult or complex information gradually may also help patients and families integrate new understanding as recovery and adjustment unfold <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Postal and Armstrong, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The function of psychoeducation may also change over time.
Early in recovery, NIPE can help patients and families understand what has happened, interpret symptoms, and reduce uncertainty.
As rehabilitation progresses, it can increasingly support engagement, strategy use, goal setting, and adjustment.
Later, NIPE can help patients and families respond to

These phases overlap rather than represent discrete stages, and the timing and content of NIPE should remain guided by the individual's circumstances and rehabilitation goals.
During acute inpatient and early post-acute care, factors such as posttraumatic amnesia, confusion, fatigue, pain, sleep disruption, and medication effects can limit new learning.

Psychoeducation may therefore be easier to process when information is provided in brief, manageable segments, revisited over time, and, where appropriate, also provided to family or other support persons (Hart et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Psychoeducation may therefore be easier to process when information is provided in brief, manageable segments, revisited over time, and, where appropriate, also provided to family or other support persons <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hart et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In mild TBI, early psychoeducation can provide information about symptoms, their expected course, and approaches to managing difficulties during recovery (Caplain et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In mild TBI, early psychoeducation can provide information about symptoms, their expected course, and approaches to managing difficulties during recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caplain et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In the subacute phase, NIPE can be integrated more directly with cognitive rehabilitation, coping and adjustment work, and goal-directed participation.
Information can be linked to emerging cognitive difficulties, rehabilitation strategies, and everyday activities as patients and families develop a clearer understanding of ongoing needs.

In stroke rehabilitation, caregiver-and dyad-focused interventions commonly combine psychoeducation with skill-building approaches such as problem solving, stress management, and goal setting (Bakas et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In stroke rehabilitation, caregiver-and dyad-focused interventions commonly combine psychoeducation with skill-building approaches such as problem solving, stress management, and goal setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bakas et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In the chronic phase, psychoeducation can remain relevant as new participation demands emerge, including return to work or study, driving, parenting, and changes in relationships or other roles.
Patients and families may also need to revisit earlier information as they adapt to persistent difficulties or encounter new challenges.
The TBI literature supports viewing education as an ongoing process that may need to address evolving concerns over time (Hart et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The TBI literature supports viewing education as an ongoing process that may need to address evolving concerns over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hart et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, cognition-related psychoeducation needs after stroke are evident throughout the post-stroke continuum and may change over time as patients and families encounter different concerns and demands (Hobden et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, cognition-related psychoeducation needs after stroke are evident throughout the post-stroke continuum and may change over time as patients and families encounter different concerns and demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hobden et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The context in which NIPE is delivered after acquired brain injury (ABI) may influence whether information is understood, remembered, and applied in everyday life.

Relevant considerations include the format of delivery, such as in person, via telehealth, self-guided, standalone, or embedded within a broader intervention, as well as who participates in the psychoeducation process.
NIPE may be delivered in person or via telehealth, either as a discrete intervention or as part of ongoing cognitive rehabilitation.

Neuropsychological feedback, for example, is commonly delivered in a single 30-to 60-minute session (McRae et al., 2024), whereas NIPE can also be incorporated across rehabilitation sessions as questions, goals, and needs emerge.
text.formatted: Neuropsychological feedback, for example, is commonly delivered in a single 30-to 60-minute session <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(McRae et al., 2024)</ref>, whereas NIPE can also be incorporated across rehabilitation sessions as questions, goals, and needs emerge.

text.text: This allows neuroscience-informed explanations to be revisited and linked to rehabilitation strategies and everyday experiences over time.
Self-guided digital formats are another option.
The choice of format should reflect the individual's cognitive abilities, preferences, access to technology, and need for clinician or family involvement.

Family members or other support persons can be included in NIPE because they may have their own psychoeducation needs and can assist with understanding and implementation when cognitive difficulties affect learning, memory, or follow-through (Hart et al., 2018; Gruters et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Family members or other support persons can be included in NIPE because they may have their own psychoeducation needs and can assist with understanding and implementation when cognitive difficulties affect learning, memory, or follow-through <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hart et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gruters et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: They may also help the person remember information, structure routines, and apply strategies in everyday settings.

Greater family involvement during inpatient TBI rehabilitation has been associated with better community participation and some cognitive functional outcomes after discharge, while caregiver-and dyad-focused interventions following stroke have shown benefits for some caregiver and stroke-survivor outcomes (Bogner et al., 2019; Bakas et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Greater family involvement during inpatient TBI rehabilitation has been associated with better community participation and some cognitive functional outcomes after discharge, while caregiver-and dyad-focused interventions following stroke have shown benefits for some caregiver and stroke-survivor outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bogner et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bakas et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Family involvement may be particularly useful when insight, memory, or executive functioning is limited, although the appropriate level of involvement should be tailored to the individual and clinical context.
Other rehabilitation professionals can also be involved when this promotes consistency in explanations, goals, and recommendations across disciplines (Larsson-Lund et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Other rehabilitation professionals can also be involved when this promotes consistency in explanations, goals, and recommendations across disciplines <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Larsson-Lund et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although much of the evidence regarding therapeutic and relational factors comes from psychotherapy rather than NIPE specifically, therapeutic outcomes are influenced not only by specific interventions but also by contextual factors such as the therapeutic alliance, collaboration, shared goals, and expectations about change (Norcross and Lambert, 2018; Wampold, 2015).
text.formatted: Although much of the evidence regarding therapeutic and relational factors comes from psychotherapy rather than NIPE specifically, therapeutic outcomes are influenced not only by specific interventions but also by contextual factors such as the therapeutic alliance, collaboration, shared goals, and expectations about change <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Norcross and Lambert, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Wampold, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These factors are particularly relevant to NIPE because explanations about brain injury, cognitive difficulties, prognosis, and rehabilitation can be personally and emotionally significant.
Clinicians therefore need to balance realistic discussion of difficulties and uncertainty with warmth, support, and appropriate hope (Postal and Armstrong, 2013; Waldron-Perrine et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Clinicians therefore need to balance realistic discussion of difficulties and uncertainty with warmth, support, and appropriate hope <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Postal and Armstrong, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Waldron-Perrine et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These therapeutic factors are reflected in several NIPE structural principles, including trustworthiness, interaction, salience, and motivation.
Goal setting and self-awareness are also considered because they can help connect NIPE with rehabilitation goals and action.
Trustworthiness in NIPE depends on more than factual accuracy.
It may be strengthened by clarity, transparency, consistency, and relevance to the patient's experience (Armstrong et al., 2024; Hart et al., 2018; Gruters et al., 2022).
text.formatted: It may be strengthened by clarity, transparency, consistency, and relevance to the patient's experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Armstrong et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hart et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gruters et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians can support trust by linking explanations to everyday difficulties, providing a coherent formulation that acknowledges cognitive, emotional, and contextual influences, and making recommendations that are feasible in daily life.
Trust also requires appropriate acknowledgement of uncertainty.
Recovery trajectories following ABI are variable, and clinicians should distinguish what is known from what remains uncertain rather than convey unwarranted confidence (Hart et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Recovery trajectories following ABI are variable, and clinicians should distinguish what is known from what remains uncertain rather than convey unwarranted confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hart et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Consistency across the rehabilitation team may further support credibility when patients and families receive compatible explanations, goals, and recommendations.
NIPE can be delivered collaboratively rather than as a one-way transfer of information.

Interactive approaches allow patients to ask questions, clarify misunderstandings, relate explanations to their own experiences, and develop a shared understanding of their difficulties and rehabilitation needs (Gorske and Smith, 2008).
text.formatted: Interactive approaches allow patients to ask questions, clarify misunderstandings, relate explanations to their own experiences, and develop a shared understanding of their difficulties and rehabilitation needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gorske and Smith, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Gorske and Smith's Collaborative Therapeutic Neuropsychological Assessment (CTNA) model illustrates this approach.

The clinician works from the patient's questions and goals, shares formulations in accessible language, invites the patient's response, and uses lived experience to refine a shared understanding of cognitive and functional difficulties.

The elicitprovide-elicit technique similarly involves first eliciting what the person already understands, providing additional information with permission, and then eliciting the person's response to that information (Gorske and Smith, 2008).
text.formatted: The elicitprovide-elicit technique similarly involves first eliciting what the person already understands, providing additional information with permission, and then eliciting the person's response to that information <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gorske and Smith, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: A shared explanatory model can connect information with action.

When the clinician and patient develop a mutually plausible understanding of the problem and rationale for intervention, recommendations may be more readily incorporated into the patient's own goals and plans (Wampold and Imel, 2015; Armstrong et al., 2024; Gruters et al., 2022).
text.formatted: When the clinician and patient develop a mutually plausible understanding of the problem and rationale for intervention, recommendations may be more readily incorporated into the patient's own goals and plans <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Wampold and Imel, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Armstrong et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gruters et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Additional support may be needed when impaired self-awareness limits recognition of important difficulties.
In NIPE, salience can be supported by making information meaningful, personally relevant, and connected to everyday functioning (Postal and Armstrong, 2013).
text.formatted: In NIPE, salience can be supported by making information meaningful, personally relevant, and connected to everyday functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Postal and Armstrong, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This can include linking explanations to the patient's concerns and goals, using examples from daily life, and drawing on observations or experiences that illustrate how cognitive difficulties affect functioning (Armstrong et al., 2024; Gruters et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This can include linking explanations to the patient's concerns and goals, using examples from daily life, and drawing on observations or experiences that illustrate how cognitive difficulties affect functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Armstrong et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gruters et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The clinician should also consider the patient's readiness and emotional response to the information being discussed.
Topics such as identity change, prognosis, return to work or driving, and relationship difficulties may be especially salient because they are emotionally significant.
Information therefore needs to be relevant enough to engage attention and reflection while being paced to avoid overwhelming the patient (Hart et al., 2018; Gruters et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Information therefore needs to be relevant enough to engage attention and reflection while being paced to avoid overwhelming the patient <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hart et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gruters et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Visual supports, metaphors, and other concrete forms of explanation may further support understanding of personally meaningful information (Postal and Armstrong, 2013).
text.formatted: Visual supports, metaphors, and other concrete forms of explanation may further support understanding of personally meaningful information <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Postal and Armstrong, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Motivation and engagement are widely regarded as important in cognitive rehabilitation (Nowell et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Motivation and engagement are widely regarded as important in cognitive rehabilitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Nowell et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In ABI, impaired self-awareness, low confidence, and ambivalence about change may complicate engagement (Medley and Powell, 2010).
text.formatted: In ABI, impaired self-awareness, low confidence, and ambivalence about change may complicate engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Medley and Powell, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: NIPE may support motivation through autonomy-supportive communication, collaborative agenda setting, and neuroscience-informed explanations that provide a credible and personally relevant rationale for rehabilitation.
Motivational interviewing (MI) provides one useful framework because it emphasises collaboration, evocation, and respect for autonomy (Medley and Powell, 2010).
text.formatted: Motivational interviewing (MI) provides one useful framework because it emphasises collaboration, evocation, and respect for autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Medley and Powell, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: MI-informed approaches have been developed to support engagement after TBI (Hsieh et al., 2012) and have been feasibly incorporated into goal setting in broader rehabilitation settings (Wintle et al., 2026).
text.formatted: MI-informed approaches have been developed to support engagement after TBI <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hsieh et al., 2012)</ref> and have been feasibly incorporated into goal setting in broader rehabilitation settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Wintle et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, NIPE may support motivation when explanations are linked to concerns and priorities that matter to the individual and to actions they can realistically undertake.
Goal setting can help translate psychoeducation into action by connecting information about cognitive difficulties and rehabilitation to personally meaningful outcomes.

Commonly identified principles of goal setting in ABI rehabilitation include collaboration, client-centredness, realistic and measurable goals, and explicit links between goals and therapy activities (Prescott et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Commonly identified principles of goal setting in ABI rehabilitation include collaboration, client-centredness, realistic and measurable goals, and explicit links between goals and therapy activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Prescott et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In NIPE, goal setting can clarify why particular strategies are relevant, where they should be used, and how progress will be evaluated.

The INCOG 2.0 guidelines similarly incorporate goal identification and psychoeducation within metacognitive strategy instruction, reflecting the importance of linking strategies to the situations in which they will be needed and anticipating barriers to their implementation (Jeffay et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The INCOG 2.0 guidelines similarly incorporate goal identification and psychoeducation within metacognitive strategy instruction, reflecting the importance of linking strategies to the situations in which they will be needed and anticipating barriers to their implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Jeffay et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Self-awareness refers to an individual's awareness of their own thoughts, actions, and cognitive functioning (Stuss, 1991).
text.formatted: Self-awareness refers to an individual's awareness of their own thoughts, actions, and cognitive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Stuss, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Impaired awareness of deficits is common following ABI and may reduce recognition of the need for rehabilitation or behaviour change (Dromer et al., 2021; Orfei et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Impaired awareness of deficits is common following ABI and may reduce recognition of the need for rehabilitation or behaviour change <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Dromer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Orfei et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Psychoeducation and feedback may help patients develop greater selfawareness by connecting cognitive difficulties with their effects on everyday functioning.

Feedback-based interventions have produced modest improvements in self-awareness after brain injury (Schmidt et al., 2011), and a recent meta-analysis found a moderate overall effect for interventions targeting self-awareness, although effects varied considerably across studies (Villalobos et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Feedback-based interventions have produced modest improvements in self-awareness after brain injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Schmidt et al., 2011)</ref>, and a recent meta-analysis found a moderate overall effect for interventions targeting self-awareness, although effects varied considerably across studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Villalobos et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For NIPE, the aim is not simply greater awareness of impairment, but an understanding that can guide realistic goals, strategy use, and participation in rehabilitation.
Cognitive difficulties following ABI can affect how new information is acquired, understood, retained, and applied.
NIPE should therefore be adapted to the individual's cognitive profile whenever possible.
Neuropsychological assessment can inform this tailoring, but several general principles are relevant even when formal assessment data are unavailable.

These include calibrating the amount and complexity of information, repeating important material, using clear and concrete language, linking new information to existing knowledge, checking understanding, and providing information through multiple modalities.
Difficulties with attention, memory, processing speed, and fatigue can make it challenging for people with ABI to take in large amounts of information at one time.
NIPE should therefore be delivered at a pace and level of complexity that reduces cognitive load while allowing sufficient opportunity for questions and discussion.

Practitioner surveys suggest that neuropsychological feedback sessions commonly last approximately 30-60 min (Varela et al., 2024; McRae et al., 2024), but session length alone does not determine appropriate intensity.
text.formatted: Practitioner surveys suggest that neuropsychological feedback sessions commonly last approximately 30-60 min <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Varela et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">McRae et al., 2024)</ref>, but session length alone does not determine appropriate intensity.

text.text: The amount, pace, and complexity of information should be tailored to the person's cognitive abilities, fatigue, emotional state, and learning needs.
Some individuals may benefit from shorter sessions or information divided across multiple contacts, whereas others may be able to engage with more detailed explanations.
Repeated exposure to important information can support learning and memory when cognitive impairment makes acquisition of new information more difficult.
In NIPE, this may occur within a session by revisiting key concepts, or across sessions by returning to important information over time.
People with moderate to severe TBI may require additional learning trials to acquire new information (DeLuca et al., 2000).
text.formatted: People with moderate to severe TBI may require additional learning trials to acquire new information <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(DeLuca et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The amount and frequency of repetition should therefore be tailored to the individual's cognitive profile and preferences, as excessive repetition may feel unnecessary or condescending.
Checking the person's understanding and comfort with the pace and amount of information can help determine how much repetition is useful.
Follow-up or booster NIPE sessions may provide opportunities to revisit important information when material from an initial session is not well retained.

Providing a written reminder following neuropsychological feedback improved recall of recommendations among caregivers, although not among patients, and did not improve adherence to recommendations (Meth et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Providing a written reminder following neuropsychological feedback improved recall of recommendations among caregivers, although not among patients, and did not improve adherence to recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Meth et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Multi-session rehabilitation interventions can also provide repeated opportunities for education, strategy practice, and feedback (Bakas et al., 2022; Fleming et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Multi-session rehabilitation interventions can also provide repeated opportunities for education, strategy practice, and feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bakas et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fleming et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because psychoeducation needs may change over time, NIPE may be best viewed as an ongoing process in which key information is revisited as recovery, goals, and circumstances evolve (Hart et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Because psychoeducation needs may change over time, NIPE may be best viewed as an ongoing process in which key information is revisited as recovery, goals, and circumstances evolve <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hart et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Communication should take account of both pre-existing language abilities and cognitive-communication difficulties following ABI.

Neuroscience terminology can be unfamiliar even across professional disciplines and may be particularly difficult for patients when combined with impairments in attention, memory, processing speed, or language.
NIPE should therefore use plain language whenever possible and introduce technical terminology only when it adds useful understanding.
The level of abstraction should also be tailored to the individual.
Concrete explanations and examples are generally useful when abstraction or executive functioning is impaired.

Metaphors can sometimes make complex ideas easier to understand and remember, but figurative language also places demands on pragmatic language and executive processes and may be misunderstood by some people with ABI (Thoma and Daum, 2006; Yang et al., 2010; Zimmermann et al., 2011; Fujimoto et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Metaphors can sometimes make complex ideas easier to understand and remember, but figurative language also places demands on pragmatic language and executive processes and may be misunderstood by some people with ABI <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Thoma and Daum, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Yang et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Zimmermann et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fujimoto et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Metaphors should therefore be used selectively and checked for understanding.
Whenever possible, explanations should be linked to concrete examples from the person's daily life.
Demonstrating how a strategy is used can also complement verbal description (Postal and Armstrong, 2013).
text.formatted: Demonstrating how a strategy is used can also complement verbal description <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Postal and Armstrong, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Drawing on broader learning theory, new information may be easier to understand when it can be connected to what the person already knows.
Meaningful learning approaches therefore emphasise linking new concepts to existing knowledge, beliefs, and experiences rather than presenting information in isolation (Bryce and Blown, 2024).
text.formatted: Meaningful learning approaches therefore emphasise linking new concepts to existing knowledge, beliefs, and experiences rather than presenting information in isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bryce and Blown, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In NIPE, the clinician can begin by identifying the patient's current understanding of the injury, cognitive difficulties, and rehabilitation, and then build from that starting point.
Linking explanations to familiar experiences and everyday examples can make new information easier to integrate while reducing large conceptual leaps that may interfere with comprehension.
This process also supports development of a shared explanatory model that can be revised as the patient's understanding develops (Gruters et al., 2022; Armstrong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This process also supports development of a shared explanatory model that can be revised as the patient's understanding develops <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Gruters et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Armstrong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Teach-back is a structured method for checking whether important information has been understood.

The clinician asks the patient or caregiver to explain key information or instructions in their own words, clarifies misunderstandings, and checks understanding again as needed (Talevski et al., 2020; Shersher et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The clinician asks the patient or caregiver to explain key information or instructions in their own words, clarifies misunderstandings, and checks understanding again as needed <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Talevski et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Shersher et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: It is typically framed as a check on the clinician's explanation rather than a test of the patient.

In practice, teach-back involves presenting a small number of essential points in clear language, asking the person to explain what they understood or how they will apply the information, and then clarifying or rephrasing as necessary.

Across diverse healthcare settings, teach-back has been associated with improvements in knowledge, skills, self-care behaviours, and some health outcomes (Talevski et al., 2020; Shersher et al., 2021; Yen and Leasure, 2019).
text.formatted: Across diverse healthcare settings, teach-back has been associated with improvements in knowledge, skills, self-care behaviours, and some health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Talevski et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Shersher et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Yen and Leasure, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Although this evidence is not specific to ABI or NIPE, teach-back provides a practical method for identifying misunderstandings before they interfere with implementation.
NIPE may be delivered using multiple modalities and media to support accessibility, retention, and opportunities for review.
Multimodal approaches present information in more than one form, such as combining verbal explanations with written or visual material.

In a randomised study of neuropsychological feedback, supplemental written information in addition to oral feedback resulted in better recall of recommendations at one-month follow-up than oral feedback alone (Fallows and Hilsabeck, 2013).
text.formatted: In a randomised study of neuropsychological feedback, supplemental written information in addition to oral feedback resulted in better recall of recommendations at one-month follow-up than oral feedback alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fallows and Hilsabeck, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Multimedia approaches, including video, web modules, apps, and telehealth platforms, provide ways to present information that can be revisited, shared with family, and standardised across services.

For example, a protocol for the MyTBI online psychoeducation platform describes approximately six brief modules (range 4-8) addressing psychosocial challenges across acute, post-acute, and chronic phases of TBI recovery (Troeung et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, a protocol for the MyTBI online psychoeducation platform describes approximately six brief modules (range 4-8) addressing psychosocial challenges across acute, post-acute, and chronic phases of TBI recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Troeung et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Video-based approaches have also been evaluated in stroke education.

MyStroke was associated with greater satisfaction with stroke education and better identification of the cause of the individual's stroke, while Movies4Stroke used brief educational films delivered through a mobile app to stroke survivor-caregiver dyads (Favilla et al., 2024; Kamal et al., 2020).
text.formatted: MyStroke was associated with greater satisfaction with stroke education and better identification of the cause of the individual's stroke, while Movies4Stroke used brief educational films delivered through a mobile app to stroke survivor-caregiver dyads <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Favilla et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kamal et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Video teach-back has also been associated with improvements in caregiver outcomes and some patient outcomes following stroke (Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Video teach-back has also been associated with improvements in caregiver outcomes and some patient outcomes following stroke <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although these studies do not directly evaluate NIPE, they illustrate ways in which multimedia can be used to supplement interactive patient and caregiver education.
Patient narratives and documentaries about living with ABI may also supplement NIPE by illustrating cognitive, emotional, and functional changes in everyday life.

Carefully selected examples may provide material for discussing adjustment, identity, and recovery, but should complement rather than replace evidence-based information about brain injury, rehabilitation, and the variability of recovery trajectories.
Taken together, these elements can be translated into a brief clinical framework for delivering NIPE during cognitive rehabilitation: Clinical implementation of NIPE in cognitive rehabilitation 1.
Assess understanding and capacity.
Assess the patient's current understanding, concerns, goals, and cognitive capacity.
Select salient neuroscience concepts.
Identify a small number of concepts that are directly relevant to the patient's current difficulties or rehabilitation goals.
Connect concepts to everyday functioning.
Link the explanation to a concrete everyday experience or functional difficulty.
Connect the explanation to a rehabilitation strategy.
Explain why the strategy is being recommended and when it may be useful.
Adapt delivery.
Present information at an appropriate pace and use written, visual, or other supports as needed.
Check understanding.
Use teach-back or another collaborative method to identify and clarify misunderstandings.
Revisit and refine.
Return to the explanation and strategy over time as understanding, recovery, and rehabilitation goals evolve.
Neuroscience-informed explanations of the mechanisms of injury and associated neurocognitive and neurobehavioural consequences of ABI are addressed elsewhere in this volume.
This section therefore focuses on NIPE related to neuroplasticity, prognosis and recovery, and rehabilitation interventions.

The aim is not to provide a comprehensive review of the neuroscience of recovery, but to identify concepts that can help patients and families understand what recovery may involve, why rehabilitation strategies are recommended, and how improvement can occur through restoration, compensation, and adaptation.
Neuroplasticity is an important concept for understanding recovery and rehabilitation following ABI.
Broadly, it refers to the capacity of the nervous system to change in response to experience, learning, injury, and other influences (Kleim and Jones, 2008; Nudo, 2011).
text.formatted: Broadly, it refers to the capacity of the nervous system to change in response to experience, learning, injury, and other influences <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kleim and Jones, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Nudo, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Plasticity can occur through changes at synaptic, cellular, and network levels and provides a biological basis for learning and adaptation.
Within NIPE, however, neuroplasticity should not be presented as synonymous with recovery or as evidence that any particular intervention will restore impaired neural systems.

Neural change is difficult to measure directly in routine clinical settings, and improvements in everyday functioning can occur through multiple pathways, including biological recovery, relearning, compensatory strategy use, environmental modification, and adjustment.
Neuroplasticity is therefore most useful as an explanatory framework for the brain's capacity for change rather than as a promise of neural restoration.

The type and extent of change following ABI depend on many factors, including the nature and severity of injury, time since injury, the cognitive function involved, prior abilities, health and psychosocial factors, and the rehabilitation experiences available to the individual.
NIPE should therefore present neuroplasticity alongside the substantial variability in recovery across people and cognitive domains.

Experience-expectant plasticity is primarily a developmental concept describing neural processes that anticipate species-typical environmental input during sensitive periods of development (Greenough et al., 1987; Nelson, 2024).
text.formatted: Experience-expectant plasticity is primarily a developmental concept describing neural processes that anticipate species-typical environmental input during sensitive periods of development <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Greenough et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Nelson, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Following brain injury, periods of heightened biological responsiveness have sometimes been compared with these developmental processes.
Evidence from stroke motor rehabilitation, for example, suggests that responsiveness to rehabilitation can vary according to the timing of intervention (Dromerick et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Evidence from stroke motor rehabilitation, for example, suggests that responsiveness to rehabilitation can vary according to the timing of intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Dromerick et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These findings provide a rationale for considering timing in rehabilitation, but they should be applied cautiously to cognitive rehabilitation.
Evidence for discrete critical or sensitive periods specifically in cognitive recovery following ABI remains limited.
NIPE should therefore avoid implying that a narrow opportunity for cognitive recovery will be permanently lost if rehabilitation does not occur within a particular timeframe.
Experience-dependent plasticity refers to neural change associated with an individual's experiences and learning across the lifespan.

This concept is directly relevant to rehabilitation because cognitive rehabilitation involves structured opportunities for learning, practice, strategy use, and adaptation (Kleim and Jones, 2008; Bayley et al., 2023). Kleim and Jones (2008) described several principles of experiencedependent plasticity relevant to rehabilitation, including the familiar idea of "use it or lose it," as well as specificity, repetition, intensity, salience, timing, transference, and interference.

text.text: These principles provide useful ways of explaining why targeted and meaningful practice matters in rehabilitation.

However, they should not be interpreted as universal rules of cognitive recovery, because much of the supporting evidence derives from basic neuroscience and motor rehabilitation, and the extent to which individual principles generalise to cognitive rehabilitation varies.
For NIPE, the most useful message is therefore not simply that patients should "use" a cognitive function more intensively.

Rather, learning is more likely to be useful when practice is targeted, meaningful, appropriately challenging, repeated sufficiently, and linked to the situations in which the skill or strategy will ultimately be needed.
The amount and timing of practice should also be balanced against fatigue, cognitive overload, and other individual factors.
Functional improvement may reflect both changes in underlying abilities and increasingly effective use of compensatory strategies and environmental supports.

The World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework emphasises that functioning and disability reflect interactions among health conditions, personal factors, and environmental factors (World Health Organization, 2001).
text.formatted: The World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework emphasises that functioning and disability reflect interactions among health conditions, personal factors, and environmental factors <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Following ABI, relevant factors may include cognitive and emotional functioning, psychosocial support, health behaviours, and the opportunities and demands present in the person's environment.
These factors vary considerably across individuals and over time and may contribute to the heterogeneity of recovery trajectories.
NIPE can help patients and families understand how modifiable factors may affect cognitive functioning and participation in rehabilitation.

Sleep disturbance can exacerbate cognitive difficulties and fatigue following ABI (Pilon et al., 2021), while physical activity may contribute to broader physical and cognitive health within stroke rehabilitation (Li et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Sleep disturbance can exacerbate cognitive difficulties and fatigue following ABI <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Pilon et al., 2021)</ref>, while physical activity may contribute to broader physical and cognitive health within stroke rehabilitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Li et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The purpose of NIPE in this context is not to imply that lifestyle factors determine recovery, but to help patients identify factors that may support functioning and rehabilitation within the context of their individual needs and circumstances.
Depression and anxiety are common following both TBI and stroke (Chun et al., 2022; Robinson et al., 2024; Dehbozorgi et al., 2024a Dehbozorgi et al., , 2024b)).
text.formatted: Depression and anxiety are common following both TBI and stroke <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chun et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Robinson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dehbozorgi et al., 2024a</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dehbozorgi et al., , 2024b))</ref>.

text.text: These symptoms may interact with sleep, fatigue, motivation, and cognitive functioning and can complicate participation in rehabilitation.
NIPE can help patients understand these interactions and why identifying and addressing psychological symptoms may support participation in cognitive rehabilitation.

More broadly, presenting recovery as the product of interacting neurological, psychological, behavioural, and environmental influences can support realistic expectations while identifying areas in which patients and families may be able to take constructive action.
A useful distinction in NIPE following ABI is between spontaneous biological recovery and improvement associated with rehabilitation, learning, compensation, and adaptation.
Spontaneous biological recovery refers to improvement associated with endogenous post-injury processes occurring in the absence of a specific targeted rehabilitation intervention.
Following stroke, these processes can include resolution of oedema and diaschisis, restoration of perfusion and metabolism, and endogenous neural reorganisation (Nudo, 2011; Bernhardt et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Following stroke, these processes can include resolution of oedema and diaschisis, restoration of perfusion and metabolism, and endogenous neural reorganisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Nudo, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bernhardt et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Recovery trajectories vary considerably according to the nature and severity of the injury, the outcome being measured, and individual and environmental factors.
Symptoms following mild TBI often improve during the first weeks, although a substantial minority of adults experience persisting symptoms (McIntosh et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Symptoms following mild TBI often improve during the first weeks, although a substantial minority of adults experience persisting symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(McIntosh et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Recovery following moderate to severe TBI can extend over considerably longer periods.

Longitudinal TRACK-TBI studies show that functional status, cognition, psychiatric symptoms, and quality of life can continue to change years after injury, with both improvement and decline observed across individuals (Nelson et al., 2023; Brett et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Longitudinal TRACK-TBI studies show that functional status, cognition, psychiatric symptoms, and quality of life can continue to change years after injury, with both improvement and decline observed across individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Nelson et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brett et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Recovery following stroke is similarly heterogeneous.

Functional change is often most rapid during the early months, but the rate and extent of recovery differ across individuals and domains, and meaningful improvement can continue during the chronic phase (Li et al., 2024; El Husseini et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Functional change is often most rapid during the early months, but the rate and extent of recovery differ across individuals and domains, and meaningful improvement can continue during the chronic phase <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Li et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">El Husseini et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive, emotional, and participation outcomes may also follow different trajectories.
These differences make it important to distinguish population-level patterns from predictions about an individual patient.
NIPE can help patients and families understand that meaningful functional improvement does not necessarily require complete restoration of an impaired cognitive process.
A person may improve through some combination of biological recovery, relearning, compensatory strategies, environmental modification, psychological adjustment, and changes in participation.

Conversely, relatively mild cognitive impairment can have substantial functional consequences when accompanied by factors such as depression, anxiety, fatigue, sleep disturbance, pain, or environmental demands.
Prognosis therefore reflects interacting neurological, psychological, behavioural, and environmental influences rather than the severity of cognitive impairment alone.
When discussing prognosis, clinicians should generally use probabilistic rather than deterministic language.

Patients and families can be informed about typical recovery patterns while also being told that the eventual degree and timing of recovery cannot be predicted precisely for an individual (Postal and Armstrong, 2013).
text.formatted: Patients and families can be informed about typical recovery patterns while also being told that the eventual degree and timing of recovery cannot be predicted precisely for an individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Postal and Armstrong, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This approach allows clinicians to provide realistic information without unnecessarily limiting hope or implying that continued rehabilitation and adaptation are futile after a particular point in time.

NIPE can also draw attention to gains that have already occurred without minimising persistent difficulties or uncertainty about future recovery.

NIPE can also provide a framework for discussing return to cognitively demanding activities such as work, study, or driving.
Rather than relying on a fixed timetable, these decisions should consider the individual's abilities, symptoms, functional demands, safety, and response to increasing activity.
Where appropriate, graded return can provide an opportunity to increase demands while monitoring functioning and adjusting rehabilitation strategies.
Driving requires particular attention to clinical and safety considerations and should be addressed within relevant assessment and regulatory requirements.
Because TBI and stroke are common forms of acquired brain injury, many current cognitive rehabilitation guidelines focus on these conditions.
Cognitive rehabilitation has been defined as a systematic, functionally oriented service based on assessment and understanding of the person's brain-behavioural deficits (Cicerone et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Cognitive rehabilitation has been defined as a systematic, functionally oriented service based on assessment and understanding of the person's brain-behavioural deficits <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cicerone et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Broadly, cognitive rehabilitation approaches may involve restoration of impaired cognitive processes, compensation for persistent impairments, environmental modification, and adaptation to disability.

Current guidelines emphasise that interventions should be functionally relevant, meaningful to the individual, and designed to support generalisation to everyday activities (Bayley et al., 2023; Cicerone et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Current guidelines emphasise that interventions should be functionally relevant, meaningful to the individual, and designed to support generalisation to everyday activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bayley et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cicerone et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: From a NIPE perspective, these distinctions are important because they provide patients with different explanatory models for how rehabilitation may improve functioning.

Some interventions aim to strengthen or restore cognitive processes through repeated practice, whereas others reduce the functional impact of persistent impairment by teaching compensatory strategies or modifying the environment.
Explaining these distinctions can help patients understand why particular interventions are recommended and develop realistic expectations about what improvement may involve.
Restorative approaches are designed to improve an impaired cognitive process through structured and repeated practice, often using graded levels of difficulty.
Examples include interventions targeting attention, memory, processing speed, or specific cognitive skills.

Evidence suggests that gains are generally strongest for trained or closely related tasks unless treatment explicitly promotes transfer to everyday activities (Cicerone et al., 2019; Ponsford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Evidence suggests that gains are generally strongest for trained or closely related tasks unless treatment explicitly promotes transfer to everyday activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cicerone et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Ponsford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: NIPE can support restorative interventions by explaining the cognitive processes being targeted, the rationale for repeated practice, and the limits of expected generalisation.
Compensatory approaches aim to reduce the functional consequences of cognitive impairment rather than directly restore the impaired process.
Internal strategies include techniques such as mnemonic methods, prospective memory strategies, and metacognitive strategies that help individuals regulate their own behavior.

External strategies use tools or systems, such as notebooks, electronic reminders, or other assistive technologies, to reduce reliance on impaired cognitive processes (Cicerone et al., 2019; Velikonja et al., 2023).
text.formatted: External strategies use tools or systems, such as notebooks, electronic reminders, or other assistive technologies, to reduce reliance on impaired cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cicerone et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Velikonja et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The choice of strategy depends on factors such as the nature and severity of impairment, capacity for new learning, insight, motivation, and the functional context in which the strategy will be used.

NIPE may facilitate compensatory strategy use by helping patients understand why a strategy is needed, what cognitive limitation it is intended to address, and how it can support functioning in everyday situations.
This may be particularly important when compensatory approaches are initially experienced as unnecessary, burdensome, or inconsistent with the person's expectations for recovery.
Environmental approaches reduce cognitive demands by modifying the physical or social environment.
Examples include reducing distractions, organising frequently used items, and placing visual cues where they are needed.
Environmental modifications can reduce reliance on memory, attention, or self-initiated strategy use by embedding supports directly in everyday settings (Hart et al., 2019; Velikonja et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Environmental modifications can reduce reliance on memory, attention, or self-initiated strategy use by embedding supports directly in everyday settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hart et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Velikonja et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: NIPE can help patients and families understand how environmental changes reduce cognitive demands and how they can function as part of a broader rehabilitation approach.
Rehabilitation following ABI may also support adjustment to persistent cognitive, emotional, behavioural, and social consequences of injury.
Adjustment can involve changes in identity, roles, relationships, expectations, and participation and is influenced by both personal and environmental factors (Livneh, 2001; Yates, 2003).
text.formatted: Adjustment can involve changes in identity, roles, relationships, expectations, and participation and is influenced by both personal and environmental factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Livneh, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Yates, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Rehabilitation may therefore include helping individuals develop an accurate understanding of their strengths and limitations, identify workable roles and goals, and adapt to changes that cannot be fully reversed.
NIPE may contribute to adjustment by helping patients integrate the possibility of continued recovery with the use of compensation and adaptation when difficulties persist.
The strategies and activities used in cognitive rehabilitation are too numerous to review comprehensively here.

Patients may also ask whether interventions outside cognitive rehabilitation can support recovery.
Depending on the clinical context, these may include pharmacological, neuromodulatory, physical, or psychological interventions.
Evidence varies considerably across intervention types and clinical populations.

Within NIPE, the primary role of discussing these approaches is to provide an accurate and appropriately qualified explanation of their potential role in recovery rather than to review them comprehensively.

text.text: This chapter has outlined how NIPE may function as an active component of cognitive rehabilitation rather than simply as supplementary information.
Its potential clinical value lies in helping patients and families develop a coherent and usable understanding of brainbehaviour relationships, cognitive difficulties, recovery, and rehabilitation.

When neuroscience-informed explanations are linked to everyday functioning and rehabilitation strategies, they may support understanding, self-awareness, realistic expectations, engagement, and application of strategies in contexts that matter, including home, community, work or study, and relationships.
The delivery of NIPE can be guided by two complementary lenses.
The therapeutic lens emphasises warmth, alliance, collaboration, shared explanatory models, and personally meaningful goals.

The cognitioninformed lens considers how difficulties in attention, memory, processing, language, and executive functioning can affect learning and informs adaptations such as calibrating the amount and complexity of information, repeating key material, using clear and concrete language, linking new information to existing knowledge, checking understanding, and providing multimodal support.
Together, these approaches are intended to make neuroscience-informed information more understandable, relevant, and actionable.
Further research is needed to determine which components of NIPE contribute to outcomes, for whom, and under what conditions.

Greater attention to intervention specification, fidelity, and outcome measurement will be important for evaluating whether NIPE improves proximal outcomes such as understanding, self-awareness, and engagement, as well as longer-term outcomes including strategy use, participation, quality of life, and functional cognition.
